facts.fact_text: The main meeting place of Mr Ter-Petrosyan's supporters during the protest rallies from 20 February 2008 onwards was Freedom Square and the surrounding park in central Yerevan.
Several hundred demonstrators stayed around the clock at Freedom Square and the surrounding park, having set up a camp.
The rallies on 1 March 2008 involved clashes between some protesters and law enforcement officers.
On 2 March 2008 the applicant tried to enter Theatre Square in central Gyumri in order to hold a protest.
On 2 March 2008 the applicant was refused entry to Theatre Square by police officers who were stationed there for the purpose of preventing any demonstrations from taking place.
It is alleged that the applicant started calling on people who were present at Theatre Square to gather and to hold a demonstration.
Police officers ordered the applicant to leave Theatre Square and to stop inciting others to assemble.
The applicant did not obey the police officers' orders to leave Theatre Square and to stop inciting others to assemble.
On 1 March 2008 in the early morning a police operation was conducted on Freedom Square in Yerevan where several hundred demonstrators were camping.
As a result of the police operation on 1 March 2008, Freedom Square was cleared of all the demonstrators.
Later on 1 March 2008 the situation in Yerevan escalated and rallies continued throughout the city until the early morning of 2 March 2008.
The rallies on 1 March 2008 involved clashes between some protesters and law enforcement officers.
The events of 1 March 2008 resulted in ten deaths, including eight civilians.
The events of 1 March 2008 resulted in numerous injured persons.
The events of 1 March 2008 resulted in destruction of private and public property.
On 1 March 2008 the incumbent President of Armenia issued a decree declaring a state of emergency in Yerevan.
The state of emergency declared by the President of Armenia on 1 March 2008 was for a period of twenty days.
The state of emergency declared on 1 March 2008 included a prohibition on holding meetings, rallies, demonstrations, marches and other mass events in Yerevan.
On 2 March 2008 at around 12.30 p.m. the applicant arrived at Theatre Square in central Gyumri.
On 2 March 2008 the applicant tried to enter Theatre Square in central Gyumri in order to hold a protest.
On 2 March 2008 the applicant was refused entry to Theatre Square by police officers who were stationed there for the purpose of preventing any demonstrations from taking place.
It is alleged that the applicant started calling on people who were present at Theatre Square to gather and to hold a demonstration.
Police officers ordered the applicant to leave Theatre Square and to stop inciting others to assemble.
The applicant did not obey the police officers' orders to leave Theatre Square and to stop inciting others to assemble.
The applicant was taken to a police station after disobeying the police officers' orders at Theatre Square on 2 March 2008.
At the police station an administrative case was initiated against the applicant under Article 182 of the Code of Administrative Offences for disobeying the lawful orders of the police officers.
A record of an administrative offence was drawn up against the applicant at the police station.
A statement was taken from the applicant at the police station.
The applicant was released from the police station after a record of an administrative offence was drawn up and a statement was taken from him.
On 5 March 2008 the police lodged a claim with the Administrative Court seeking to subject the applicant to a penalty under Article 182 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
The police stated in their claim that the applicant had called on others to hold a demonstration at Theatre Square in Gyumri.

The police stated in their claim that the applicant had refused to obey the lawful orders of the police officers, who had been stationed at Theatre Square for the purpose of preventing the conduct of unauthorised demonstrations, to stop his actions and to leave.
The police noted in their claim that the Gyumri Mayor's Office had not been duly notified of the demonstration at Theatre Square on 2 March 2008.
The police noted in their claim that no authorisation had been obtained to hold the demonstration at Theatre Square on 2 March 2008.
On 24 March 2008 the applicant lodged a counter-claim against the police.
In his counter-claim, the applicant argued that the police had failed to substantiate the factual basis of their claim, namely the fact that he had called on others to hold a rally.
In his counter-claim, the applicant insisted that he had not intended to organise a rally and that there had not been any rally at Theatre Square at the material time.
In his counter-claim, the applicant argued that the act of calling on people was not an act prohibited and therefore punishable by law.
In his counter-claim, the applicant argued that no evidence had been produced to show that more than 100 people had gathered at or in the vicinity of Theatre Square at the material time.

In his counter-claim, the applicant argued that the allegation that he had called on others to hold a rally without prior notification was unsubstantiated, since the law did not require prior notification if fewer than 100 people took part in a rally.
In his counter-claim, the applicant argued that the police orders addressed to him could not be considered lawful.
On an unspecified date the police lodged a written response to the applicant's counter-claim, seeking to dismiss it as unsubstantiated.
The police claimed in their written response that well-known facts were not liable to be proved.

The police asserted that well-known facts included the fact that a tense situation had been created in Armenia after the tragic events of 1 March 2008, which threatened national security and public safety.

The police asserted in their written response that the day before the incident on 2 March 2008, an unauthorised rally had been held on Theatre Square in Gyumri, at which the time and place of the next rally had been announced.

The police asserted in their written response that at the unauthorised rally held the day before the incident, it had been announced that the applicant, who was known to be an active rally participant, would make a speech at Theatre Square.
The police asserted in their written response that it was not by chance that the applicant had appeared at Theatre Square on 2 March 2008, as he was not just an accidental passer-by.
The police asserted in their written response that the administrative case against the applicant was therefore justified.
On 31 March 2008 the applicant lodged his objections to the police's written response, contesting the factual allegations made by the police.
On 10 June 2008 the Administrative Court granted the police claim against the applicant.
On 10 June 2008 the Administrative Court dismissed the applicant's counter-claim against the police.

On 10 June 2008 the Administrative Court subjected the applicant to an administrative fine under Article 182 of the Code of Administrative Offences in the amount of 50,000 Armenian Drams (approximately 110 euros at the material time) for disobeying the lawful orders of the police officers.

The Administrative Court held that on 2 March 2008 at around 12 noon police officers of the Gyumri Police Station were performing their duties at Gyumri's Theatre Square and its surroundings for the purpose of prohibiting the conduct of a demonstration in respect of which no notification had been made in accordance with the procedure prescribed by law.

The Administrative Court found, referring to the requirements of Section 10 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, that there had been no legal basis for holding a demonstration at Theatre Square in Gyumri on 2 March 2008.

The Administrative Court found that on 2 March 2008 at around 12.30 p.m. the applicant arrived at Theatre Square in Gyumri and wanted to enter the square, but was prevented and ordered to leave that area and not to call on people to gather and hold an event, which he disobeyed.
The Administrative Court made reference to Sections 2, 12, 22 and 38 of the Police Act (2001).

The Administrative Court held that mass public events may be held only after notification in writing to the competent authority, in this case the Head of the Gyumri Community, in accordance with the requirements of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act.
The Administrative Court held that no notification of a mass public event on 2 March 2008 had been submitted to the Head of the Gyumri Community.

The Administrative Court noted that the President of Armenia, by Decree no. NH-35-N of 1 March 2008, declared a state of emergency in Yerevan starting from 1 March 2008 for a period of twenty days for the purpose of preventing the threat to the constitutional order of the country and protecting the rights and lawful interests of the population.

The Administrative Court found that the conduct of a mass public event in Gyumri, the second largest city of the country, could have endangered the protection of public order and public health, particularly when no notification to hold such an event had been submitted in accordance with the prescribed procedure.

The Administrative Court found that the police applied certain restrictions on gathering and holding events on Gyumri's Theatre Square pursuant to Article 43 of the Constitution of Armenia and the Police Act (2001).
The Administrative Court concluded that the orders given to the applicant, which he had disobeyed, had been lawful.

Article 43 of the Constitution of Armenia, as in force at the material time, permitted restrictions on the right to freedom of peaceful assembly under the conditions of being prescribed by law and necessary in a democratic society for the protection of national security and public order, the prevention of crimes, the protection of public health and morals, or the protection of constitutional rights and freedoms, honour and good reputation of others.

Article 182 of the Code of Administrative Offences, as in force at the material time, provided that disobeying a lawful order of a military serviceman or a police officer issued in the performance of his duties of preserving public order and of ensuring public safety would result in a fine in the amount of 50 times the fixed minimum wage.

According to Section 2 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act (2004-2011), the concept of a public event includes peaceful assemblies, rallies, marches (parades) and demonstrations (including sit-ins).
According to Section 2 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act (2004-2011), 'mass public events' are defined as public events which have 100 or more participants.
According to Section 2 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act (2004-2011), 'non-mass public events' are defined as public events which have fewer than 100 participants.

Section 10 §§ 1, 2 and 4 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act (2004-2011) provides that, except for cases when a non-mass public event spontaneously turns into a mass public event, mass public events may be held only after notifying the competent authority in writing.

Section 10 §§ 1, 2 and 4 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act (2004-2011) provides that everyone has the right to hold non-mass public events without notifying the competent authority and without violating public order.
Section 2 of the Police Act (2001) provides that the objectives of the police include the prevention of crimes and the protection of public order and public safety.

Section 12 of the Police Act (2001) provides that the police are obliged to ensure the protection of public order in the streets, squares, parks, railway stations, airports, polling stations and other public spaces, as well as during court hearings upon a court's request.
According to Section 22 of the Police Act (2001), when protecting public order, the police are entitled to restrict or ban temporarily the traffic and the pedestrian flow.

According to Section 22 of the Police Act (2001), when protecting public order, the police are entitled to oblige people to remain in specific spaces, facilities, streets or roads for the protection of their life, health or property or for the conduct of investigative or operative-search measures, and must immediately inform their superiors about this.
Section 38 of the Police Act (2001) provides that every citizen and public official is obliged to obey lawful orders of a police officer.

Section 38 of the Police Act (2001) provides that failure to obey lawful orders of a police officer or actions obstructing the performance of a police officer's duties result in liability in accordance with the procedure prescribed by law.
